Because he had been distracted making observations and a malfunction of the automatic alignment system, Carpenter overshot his planned reentry mark and splashed down 250 miles (402 kilometers) from target. USA Man here: Can someone explain why David Cameron resigned?
He called for the referendum to shut up any talk of Brexit. Now he has to preside over a Brexit he does not support. He had pretty much no other choice.
Yup, he called for it, it blew up in his face.

My attempt at an explanation (I'm not British, but Dutch so take it for what it's worth)

  1. European Prime-Ministers are only head of the government, not head of State. I guess this could make them more "replaceable" than a US president would be. Our Kings and Queens continue their day to day functions and changing a prime-minister (Tony Blair stepping down for Gordon Brown after 10 years comes to mind) is more like a cabinet-reshuffling.

  2. Most Europeans don't vote for the Prime-Minister as a person. They vote for parties (the UK does have district voting for people so I'm fuzzy on the details) and the largest party delivers a Prime-Minister and leads the formation of a government. Cameron resigning could just mean a different Tory taking his place and no new elections.

  3. As Cameron had been campaigning so hard for Remain, he might have a credibility problem. 52% of the UK population voted against a position held by their Prime-Minister. A new Prime-Minister more in line with the will of the people would be demanded by the Tories soon enough (to prevent a future electoral disaster). By taking the initiative Pork-fucker Dave is merely trying to keep dignity.

Overall our politics are slightly more fuzzy than American politics. Most European countries don't have the clear distinction between the three branches of government, Washington has. (For example in Holland the Cabinet has both executive & legislative power, while our Parliament is only "co-legislator and comptroller")
Thank you for this explanation. Likening him to more of a cabinet leader makes much more sense to me.

EUSSR-drone has the important part here. The PM is the leader of the party with majority in government, not the head of state or anything similar. The head of the party is elected by the party itself, not the people.

Cameron probably (rightly) thought that he had no hope of maintaining leadership over his party long term, after such a divisive campaign where he campaigned so hard for the losing side. The Conservative party now needs a new leader who isn't hated by half their party and who isn't too closely tied to Brussels to work through Leave negotiations.

It's been done before, but it's rarely done lightly, because the populace doesn't really like the prime minister changing without public vote, but many people wanted him out regardless, and if he hadn't there would have been a very real possibility of a vote of no confidence being passed by rebelling MPs (and MPs of the other parties), which would have forced him out of power and end the government (normally this is a 5 year thing, but a vote of no confidence would mean a general election which would mean more instability in the country)..

This was probably the best option, overall, and actually restored a glimmer of respect for the man. It preserves as much stability as possible for the country, which prevents further drops by the pound and helps reduce some of the division this referendum has caused.

The Conservative party now needs a new leader who isn't hated by half their party and who isn't too closely tied to Brussels to work through Leave negotiations.

So you think that Cameron (if he stayed) could potentially make some deals that would keep certain things in effect even though the UK is leaving the EU?

Any PM they appoint could, potentially. If they arranged for an agreement similar to Switzerland or Norway then that would potentially reinstate free, open borders again. They could fail to negotiate a real treaty at all and give back a lot of our sovereignty to the EU. Hopefully the new Prime Minister will be at least moderately Euro-skeptic to avoid this, but it's all up in the air until October at least.
